Acrylic paint-along · beginner

A striped hot-air balloon floating over a lavender field at sunset, with soft violet mountains, golden hills, and one big tree on the right.

Start on a plain white canvas. Paint the sky first, then each part of the scene from farthest to nearest, each straight over the one behind it. Then the main subject, texture with simple brush moves, shadows, and highlights last.

12 stepsCanvas: 14 x 11 inFocal point: The striped balloon, upper left (28% across, 15% down in the frame), set against the glowing orange sky. Light: The low sun, behind the mountains a little left of center (43% across, 41% down in the frame): cloud undersides and the tree's left side catch the light, and the lavender tips glow lilac and pink.How this lesson was made

What you need

Tubes

  • Titanium white
  • Medium yellow
  • Yellow ochre
  • Flesh tint
  • Permanent red
  • Rouge
  • Light magenta
  • Violet
  • Ultramarine
  • Lake blue
  • Dark green
  • Ocean green

Brushes

  • 1 inch flat: covering and blending the skyFlat: square end, for big areas and straight edges
  • #8 round: the sun discRound: pointed tip, thin or thick depending on how hard you press
  • #12 flat (or 1 inch flat): scrubbing the cloud massesFlat: square end, for big areas and straight edges
  • old stiff flat: dabbing the bushesOld stiff flat: worn, splayed bristles, for rough texture like grass and foliage
  • #4 round: band and basketRound: pointed tip, thin or thick depending on how hard you press
  • Liner (#1 or #0): the ropesLiner: long, very thin bristles, for fine lines like twigs and grass

Also

  • A 14 x 11 in canvas, landscape (hang it that way). Positions in the steps are percentages across and down: each 10% is 1.4 in across and 1.1 in down.
  • Water jar and paper towel
  • Palette or paper plate for mixing

Your paints

Every paint in the lesson. You don't have to mix them all at the start: each step lists the paints it uses with their recipes, so you can mix a little as you go before it dries. Parts are by volume.

The steps

Step 1Step 2Step 3Step 4Step 5Step 6Step 7Step 8Step 9Step 10Step 11Step 12

STEP 1 OF 12

Paint the sunset sky and the sun

  1. The light comes from the sun, low and a little left of center, 37% across and 41% down. Every highlight faces it.
  2. With the 1 inch flat and creamy Evening blue, paint the top 10% in long side-to-side strokes.
  3. Blend Sunset orange down to 45%. Brush Sun gold in a soft oval about a hand wide around the sun (25% to 50% across and down).
  4. Blend Sunset red from 45% down to a straight edge at 59%, past where the mountains go. Leave the bottom white.
  5. With the #8 round, dab a Sun cream circle about 4% wide (half an inch) into the wet gold at 37% across, 41% down.
Paints for this step5 paints, 5 new
  • Evening blue new3 parts lake blue, 2 parts white
  • Sunset orange new2 parts medium yellow, 1 part light magenta
  • Sun gold new1 part medium yellow, 1 part flesh tint
  • Sunset red new1 part medium yellow, 1 part rouge, a touch of white
  • Sun cream new3 parts white, 1 part yellow ochre, a touch of flesh tint

Colors dry a little darker, so test each mix on the palette edge first.

Mix plenty of Sunset orange; it covers half the sky.

Brushes

1 inch flat#8 round

Strokes

Long horizontal blend. Pull the flat across the whole width in long, level strokes, then stroke back over each color join while wet.

Watch out: Don't stop the sky at the mountains; run it to 59% so the strokes stay long.

Watch out: Work fast: blend only while the paint is wet, about 5 minutes.

Drying: About 10 minutes between steps (a hair dryer on low speeds it up). An hour after the last step before handling.

How this picture was made Render · free

Why this step, now: Everything sits on the sky, so it goes first and runs down to 59% so the mountains and fields can be painted over it.

Why this tool: cut from the finished painting (#8)

No diagram: A gradient: the colors are named in order with where each band sits.

STEP 2 OF 12

Lay in the coral clouds

  1. Let the sky dry first.
  2. With the #12 flat and Cloud rose, scrub small circles for the cloud tops: a big mass across the top right from 40% across, and a band on the far left 5% to 30% down.
  3. Fill the rest of each cloud with Cloud coral, still in small circles, flat bottoms toward the sun.
  4. Add a few long thin Cloud coral streaks across the middle, 25% to 38% down. Keep clear of the sun's glow.
Build the depth, dark first
ValuePaintWhere
darkCloud rosethe tops of each cloud, away from the sun
midCloud coralthe rest of each cloud
Paints for this step2 paints, 2 new
  • Cloud coral new1 part medium yellow, 1 part rouge, 1 part light magenta
  • Cloud rose new2 parts rouge, 1 part flesh tint, a touch of yellow ochre

Brushes

#12 flat (or 1 inch flat)

Strokes

Small circles. Scrub the corner of the flat in small circles with a light load, so the edges stay soft and bumpy.

Watch out: Let blue sky peek through the big mass near the top; don't fill it solid.

Drying: About 10 minutes between steps (a hair dryer on low speeds it up). An hour after the last step before handling.

Why this step, now: The clouds' dark tops and body go on before their lit edges, so the light can sit on top.

STEP 3 OF 12

Light the cloud edges

  1. Let the clouds dry first.
  2. With the #8 round and creamy Sunset orange, paint most of the big top-right mass solid in small circles, leaving Cloud rose on its topmost bumps.
  3. Pull four or five thin Sunset orange wisps on a slant, from 15% across, 25% down up to 50% across, 10% down. Let blue show between.
  4. Wipe the brush nearly dry and skim Sunset orange along every cloud's lower edge, then touch Sun gold on edges nearest the sun.
Build the depth, dark first
ValuePaintWhere
midSunset orangelower edges of every cloud
lightSun goldsmall touches on the edges nearest the sun
Paints for this step2 paints
  • Sunset orange from step 1, mix more if it has dried2 parts medium yellow, 1 part light magenta
  • Sun gold from step 1, mix more if it has dried1 part medium yellow, 1 part flesh tint

Try the nearly dry brush on scrap paper first.

Brushes

#8 round

Strokes

Small circles. Solid orange pieces: a normal load, scrubbed in small circles like the coral.

Dry brush. Thin glowing edges only: wipe the brush nearly clean and skim it lightly so the orange breaks up.

Watch out: Leave Cloud rose on the cloud tops; the dark top is what makes them look round.

Drying: About 10 minutes between steps (a hair dryer on low speeds it up). An hour after the last step before handling.

STEP 4 OF 12

Paint the far mountains

  1. Let the sky dry first.
  2. With the 1 inch flat and Far mountain violet, paint the far range: a peak at the left edge 37% down, a dip below the sun, a peak 59% across, 40% down.
  3. Fill down to about 47% with level strokes, leaving the sun round above the dip.
  4. Paint the near ridge's bumpy top, 45% to 51% down, in Ridge indigo, then Ridge blue below it to 55%, in level strokes.

1 inch flat

Strokes

Horizontal strokes. Keep the flat level and pull long strokes; slope only along the mountain tops.

Watch out: Keep the far mountains soft and plain: no texture far away.

STEP 5 OF 12

Paint the fields and the golden hill

  1. Let the mountains dry first.
  2. With the 1 inch flat, lay the far fields 50% to 63% down on the left and middle in level bands, alternating Field olive and Hill gold.
  3. Paint the hill from 63% down at 28% across up to 46% at the right edge: Field olive on its lower half, Hill gold above.
  4. Pull a few Hill light streaks along the hilltop, up the slope. Let it all dry.
  5. With the old stiff flat and Bush green, dab a low bush line 54% to 60% down on the left, and along the hill's foot.
Build the depth, dark first

Brushes

1 inch flatold stiff flat

Strokes

Strokes that follow the slope. On the hill, pull the flat up and to the right along the slope.

Dabbing. Tap the stiff brush's corner with little paint so the bushes look soft and round.

Watch out: Dab the bushes only on dry paint, or the green turns the gold muddy.

Drying: About 10 minutes between steps (a hair dryer on low speeds it up). An hour after the last step before handling.

STEP 6 OF 12

Paint the big tree

  1. Let the hill dry first.
  2. With the #8 round and Trunk brown, pull the trunk up from 47% down at 86% across to about 38%, splitting into short branches.
  3. Dab the crown with the stiff flat in Bush green, 68% across to the right edge, 22% to 44% down, in five round clumps (diagram).
  4. Dab Tree green on the top of each clump, then Tree lit green on the left, sun side.

If it looks messy now, that's the ugly stage every painting goes through. Keep going.

Brushes

#8 roundold stiff flat

Strokes

Press and lift. Press the round's belly at the trunk's base, then lift as you pull up, so the trunk tapers.

Dabbing. Tap the stiff brush in round clumps, darkest first, each lighter value covering less.

Watch out: Leave some dark showing between the lighter clumps.

Drying: About 10 minutes between steps (a hair dryer on low speeds it up). An hour after the last step before handling.

STEP 7 OF 12

Paint the hot-air balloon

  1. Let the sky dry first.
  2. With chalk, draw the teardrop as in the diagram: about 2.5 inches wide, 11% to 29% across, 4% to 27% down. Mark curved stripe lines.
  3. With the #8 round, paint the stripes left to right: red, blue, red, yellow, blue, teal, red, yellow, teal, red, thin yellow edge.
  4. Near the left and right edges, blend a little Trunk brown into each wet stripe so the sides look darker and round.
  5. With the #4 round and Trunk brown, add the bottom band and a basket at 20% across, 30% to 33% down; liner ropes between.

  • Balloon yellow new1 part medium yellow, a touch of light magenta

  • Balloon teal new2 parts ocean green, 1 part lake blue, a touch of white
  • Trunk brown from step 6, mix more if it has dried3 parts dark green, 2 parts permanent red

Rinse fully between stripe colors, or the yellow goes green.

Thin the brown like ink for the ropes, and test a line on scrap paper.

Brushes

#8 round#4 roundLiner (#1 or #0)

Strokes

Curved strokes that follow a form. Pull each stripe from top to bottom along the balloon's curve, so it looks round.

Liner work. Thin paint, brush upright, light steady pressure for the ropes.

Watch out: Stripes are widest in the middle and narrow toward the edges.

Drying: About 10 minutes between steps (a hair dryer on low speeds it up). An hour after the last step before handling.

STEP 8 OF 12

Block in the lavender rows and paths

  1. Let the fields dry first. Mark a dot at 58% across, 62% down: every row and path runs to it.
  2. With the #8 round and Path earth, paint two paths from the dot: left to 28%-38% across at the bottom edge, right to 75%-86%.
  3. With the 1 inch flat and Lavender shadow, fill the rest solid from about 61% down to the bottom, strokes running toward the dot. Let it dry.
  4. With the #4 round and Path earth, pull thin lines toward the dot to split the field into rows, thin near the dot.
Paints for this step2 paints, 2 new
  • Lavender shadow new1 part lake blue, a touch of ultramarine, a touch of permanent red
  • Path earth new3 parts yellow ochre, 2 parts light magenta, a touch of dark green

Brushes

1 inch flat#8 round#4 round

Strokes

Strokes toward a vanishing point. Pull each stroke along its row toward the dot: rows wide in front, thin near the dot.

Watch out: Keep the paths straight; they stay that shape to the end.

Drying: About 10 minutes between steps (a hair dryer on low speeds it up). An hour after the last step before handling.

How Claude read your photosubject, light, layers

Before starting

Subject: A striped hot-air balloon over a lavender field at sunset

Found in the image: just the picture

Done: none

Why: No bars, borders, or captions; the whole image is the painting.

Fitted to your canvas

Canvas: 14 x 11 in, landscape

Done: crop

Left out: about 11% on the left (cloud band, the left end of the hills and lavender) and 4% on the right

Why: The picture is wider than 14x11; plain edges could go without touching the balloon, sun, tree, or paths.

Beginner version

What made it too busy: Tiny separate things: yes, a village of houses and many cypresses. Textures of hundreds of items: yes, every lavender stalk. Detail inside big shapes: yes, veined, puffy clouds. More than 8 parts: yes, about a dozen at different distances.

Changed: Dropped the village, cypresses, and lake glint; merged the clouds into a few big masses, the farmland into two or three bands with one bush line, and the mountains into two flat layers; turned the lavender into rows of loose dabs and the tree into four or five clumps.

Why: A beginner can't paint a village or thousands of stalks; the composition, balloon, sun, tree, and converging rows are what make the picture.

A sunset scene built in bands: a hot orange and coral sky, soft violet mountains, golden hills with one big tree, and a lavender field whose rows run to a vanishing point. The balloon is the subject but small; the hard parts for a beginner are the cloud values, keeping the rows and paths converging on one dot, and building the lavender texture in passes instead of all at once.

Subject: A striped hot-air balloon floating over a lavender field at sunset, with soft violet mountains, golden hills, and one big tree on the right.
Focal point: The striped balloon, upper left (28% across, 15% down in the frame), set against the glowing orange sky.
Light: The low sun, behind the mountains a little left of center (43% across, 41% down in the frame): cloud undersides and the tree's left side catch the light, and the lavender tips glow lilac and pink.

What it saw, back to front

  1. sky gradient and sun
  2. coral cloud masses
  3. lit cloud edges
  4. far mountains
  5. far fields, bush line, and golden hill

Why this techniquePaint along, back to front

The owner named the technique (acrylic-paint-along-beginner).

ChosenPaint along, back to frontStart on a plain white canvas. Paint the sky first, then each part of the scene from farthest to nearest, each straight over the one behind it. Then the main subject, texture with simple brush moves, shadows, and highlights last.

Paint-along, back to front, fits a layered landscape exactly: sky, clouds, mountains, fields, tree, balloon, then the foreground lavender, each over the one behind.

Passed onBlock in, then build up (acrylic-block-in-beginner)

It starts with a toned ground, a sketch, and a block-in of every area; the owner paints YouTube-style paint-alongs, and this picture's bands go on naturally back to front.

How the paint recipes were worked out27 paints, free

Paint doesn't mix like light on a screen: blue and yellow make green, not gray. So the recipes come from a pigment mixing model (Mixbox), not a guess. For each paint it tried every simple recipe from your tubes, up to three colors plus white, and kept the one that lands closest to the color in the painting. Delta E is how far off it lands: under 2 is hard to see, under 5 is close, and over 8 means these tubes can't quite make it.

Why the steps go in this order12 steps

Back to front: the sky runs past the mountains so its strokes stay long, then clouds (dark, then lit edges), mountains, fields and hill, the tree on the hill, the balloon over the finished sky, and the lavender last because it is nearest. The lavender is built in passes: flat dark rows, dark stem dabs, violet dabs, lighter violet spikes, and lilac tips in the final step.

  1. 1. Paint the sunset sky and the sun

    Everything sits on the sky, so it goes first and runs down to 59% so the mountains and fields can be painted over it.

  2. 2. Lay in the coral clouds

    The clouds' dark tops and body go on before their lit edges, so the light can sit on top.

  3. 3. Light the cloud edges

    The sun-facing edges come last for the clouds, after the coral is dry.

  4. 4. Paint the far mountains

    The farthest land, soft and plain, right over the sky.

  5. 5. Paint the fields and the golden hill

    The middle distance, over the mountains' base; the tree's hill must be there before the tree.

  6. 6. Paint the big tree

    Sits on the hill, so it follows it; dark, mid, then lit clumps.

  7. 7. Paint the hot-air balloon

    The subject; it floats in the sky, so it goes on once the sky and everything behind it are dry.

  8. 8. Block in the lavender rows and paths

    The nearest area. Its rows and paths are laid flat first so the converging lines are set before any texture.

  9. 9. Dab the dark lavender

    Inserted by split-texture: the darkest marks first, so the lavender doesn't jump from flat to textured.

  10. 10. Dab the middle violet

    Inserted by split-texture: the first violet pass over the dark.

  11. 11. Dab the lighter violet on top

    The lighter violet on the clump tops, so each row reads as rounded bushes.

  12. 12. Add the lavender tips and final highlights

    Lilac tips: the brightest marks, last.

Filters it tried5 free looks
Where Claude drew diagrams4 steps, free

Four steps needed pictures: the tree and the balloon are shaped objects appearing whole, the rows depend on one vanishing point, and the lavender clump is a repeated mark that has to be built up stroke by stroke.

  • Step 6: Paint the big tree beginner check

    Noticed: A shaped object appears whole, and where the crown starts and how the trunk forks isn't clear from the picture.

    Pieces: A Y trunk, then six round dark clumps (one small one sticking out left), mid green on the tops, lit green on the left facing the sun.

  • Step 7: Paint the hot-air balloon beginner check

    Noticed: The subject appears whole; the teardrop outline and curved stripes need sketching first.

    Pieces: A circle for the top, a taper to a point, curved stripe guide lines from top to bottom, then the band, ropes, and basket.

  • Step 8: Block in the lavender rows and paths beginner check

    Noticed: The rows' and paths' placement depends on one vanishing point, which an instruction can't show well.

    Pieces: A dot at 58% across, the two paths widening from it, then thin row lines fanning out from it, drawn at the field's real proportions (a wide, short band).

  • Step 11: Dab the lighter violet on top beginner check

    Noticed: A repeated mark across the whole field; the step review showed the marks are flicked spikes, not dots.

    Pieces: One front clump: the dark base and violet body already painted, then spikes flicked up and out from the middle, then where the lilac tips go in the last step.

What Claude would do differentlyfor the next lesson
  • Every first-round render of a cloud step stopped the sky at the sun (a wavy edge 41-47% down) even though looks_like gave a straight edge at 65%; the redo prompt saying 'the sky must not stop at the sun' worked.
  • A lock-steps protect box over the sun didn't help in the glow step: the step's own paints (Sun gold, Sunset orange) were allowed to change it. Leaving the sun out of the step's regions (boxes around it) did. In the mountains step a protect box left a visible rectangle; splitting the region around the sun fixed it.
  • split-texture copies the parent step's paints, looks_like, and colors to the new in-between steps (looks_like prefixed 'pass N of 3 toward'), so the darkest pass was labeled 'medium violet dabs' with Lavender violet. Every inserted step needs its plan entry rewritten by hand; the tool could name the passes dark and mid itself.
  • The darkest split-texture pass used a color darker than the base rows (the dark stems in the finish), so its paint had to be a new, darker mix (Lavender deep); the plan's base-row color alone couldn't make it.
  • canvas-view given a path (output/<lesson>/99_finish.png) instead of a file name inside the lesson reported success with a nested canvas/output/... path but wrote nothing. It should refuse or resolve the path.
  • canvas/ keeps stale crops after split-texture renumbers steps (a canvas/09_lavender-dabs.png stayed after the step became 11); publish doesn't clear them.
  • The mixer's recipes for some paints ignore the obvious straight tubes (Trunk brown as dark green plus permanent red instead of burnt umber and burnt sienna; Sunset orange as medium yellow plus light magenta). They hit the swatch (Delta E about 1) but read oddly to a painter who owns those tubes.
  • The step review says lavender in this style is flicked spikes, not dabs; the plan's 'dabs' wording came from the beginner-version prompt. Research section 4 covers fields and grass (flicking) but not flower clumps like lavender; worth a note there.
  • The step review flagged lavender clumps overhanging the paths as a shape change. They overhang in the finish too, so I skipped it; step-review.md could say that foreground texture overlapping a path's edge isn't a change to the path.
